title: Pacers star Tyrese Haliburton moved to tears following first game back from Achilles tear - CBS Sports
description: Haliburton played in his first non-preseason game since Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals
body:
Haliburton played in his first non-preseason game since Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:46 am ET

            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Pacers star Tyrese Halliburton returned to the court in a non-preseason setting for the first time in 486 days on Wednesday as Indiana opened its season with a 123-120 win over the Pelicans. Haliburton, who tore his Achilles tendon during Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals against the Thunder, didn't play last season while recovering from the injury.While being interviewed by Pacers sideline reporter Jeremiah Johnson after the win, Haliburton was moved to tears as he talked about his return to the court."It means a lot to be back out here," Haliburton said. "... I'm just really thankful to be back out here."
Haliburton finished with 23 points, 12 assists, two rebounds and a steal in 34 minutes of action and had a clutch play down the stretch to give his team the lead back for good after trailing by as many as 10 points. With 1:25 remaining, Haliburton had the ball at the top of the arc, crossed over left, took the contact from Zion Williamson in the paint and finished with a left-handed floater that resulted in a three-point play. Haliburton scored 16 of his 23 points in the fourth quarter.
The Pelicans had multiple attempts to tie the game during their penultimate offensive possession, but Jeremiah Fears and Williamson both missed. With Haliburton sidelined, the Pacers went 19-63 last season, including losing 13 of their first 14, but are expected to bounce back and contend in a loaded Eastern Conference.

Hello football friends, and welcome to the Thursday edition of the Pick Six newsletter! We had some big news drop here at CBS Sports today: JJ Watt has signed a new deal that officially makes him the lead analyst in our No. 1 NFL booth with Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson. The new deal means that Watt will be in the announcer's booth for Super Bowl LXII next season. For those of you scoring at home, that is only 479 days away. Watt has been with CBS Sports since 2023, when he was hired as a studio analyst on "The NFL Today." In 2025, he made the move to the announcer's booth, where he teamed up with Ian Eagle and Evan Washburn. And now, he's in the top booth. 
Not only does he crush it in the broadcast booth, but Watt is also an extremely entertaining guy to follow on social media, so I'd suggest you follow him on Instagram or even X. And now, let's get back to our normal newsletter business. As always, here's your daily reminder to tell all of your friends to sign up for the newsletter. To get them signed up, just click here. Let's get to the rundown.   1. Thursday night preview: Picks and best bets for Patriots at Bears
                                                                    Quinn Harris/Getty Images
                                                            The Bears only have one Super Bowl win in franchise history, and it came over the Patriots back in 1985. The reason I'm bringing that up now is that the Bears will be honoring Mike Ditka tonight, and he was the coach of that 1985 team. This is the team's first home game since Ditka's passing on Oct. 9, so the Bears will be celebrating his life. Good luck, Patriots. 
On the injury front, the Patriots are banged up going into this game, especially on the offensive line. They'll be down two starters with starting guards Alijah Vera-Tucker and Ben Brown both ruled out. As for the Bears, they'll be missing Kyle Monangai for the third straight game. Now that we've got that out of the way, here's one reason why each team should be feeling confident going into the game:  Why the Patriots can win: Since the start of last season, no quarterback has been better at throwing deep passes than Drake Maye. The Patriots QB has completed 56% of his passes and thrown 16 TD passes on throws of 15 air yards or more in that span. Now, he gets to go up against a Bears defense that has been the worst in the NFL at stopping long passes. Dating back to the start of the 2025 season and through this week, the Bears have ranked dead last in the NFL in completion percentage on long passes and in touchdowns allowed (17). If the Patriots get their long ball going tonight, they might be able to pull off the upset.Why the Bears can win: This might be a situation where the Bears can just let the Patriots beat themselves. This game is being played in Chicago, and the Patriots have been bad on the road this year. They've turned the ball over eight times in just three games, with six of those coming on interceptions from Drake Maye. The Bears are 3-0 this season in any game where they've forced a turnover, so they need to be opportunistic tonight. It would also help the Bears to get their running game going. Only one team has topped 100 yards on the Patriots this year, and that came in Week 3 when the Jags destroyed New England 35-6. The Bears have the top rushing attack in the NFL, and if they get that going, it's hard to see them losing this game. You can get a full preview of the game from Jared Dubin by clicking here. If you're thinking about betting on the game, here are a couple of props.  ONE RECEIVING PROP I LIKE: A.J. Brown OVER 5.5 receptions (+111 at DraftKings): In his return to the lineup on Sunday, Brown got targeted 10 times, and we could see a similar number in Chicago, given the Patriots' banged-up receiver room. Brown did uncharacteristically drop three passes against the Jets on Sunday, and I have to think he'll want to make up for that, so I won't be surprised if he has a big night.  ONE KICKING PROP I LIKE: Andres Borregalas OVER 6.5 points (-125 at DraftKings): The Patriots have a high-powered offense, but they've struggled to score in the red zone, ranking just 18th in the NFL in red zone TD percentage. That means there should be ample scoring opportunities for Borregalas in this game. Also, the Bears have played three home games this year, and the road kicker is averaging 7.3 points per game in those three matchups.  If you're wondering how my props are doing this year, I'm 8-16 (3-9 on kicker props and 5-7 on all other props). After starting off 5-3, I'm now 3-13 on my last 16 props. It has been a NIGHTMARE. This is all clearly a sign that you should be fading me until further notice.
And now, it's time for some picks.  PICKS FOR 'TNF' Jared Dubin's pick: Bears 31-27 over Patriots John Breech's pick: Bears 27-20 over PatriotsJordan Dajani's pick: Bears 28-24 over Patriots Tyler Sullivan's pick: Bears 24-20 over Patriots Prisco's pick: Patriots 28-27 over BearsIf you want to know which way all of our experts are leaning tonight, you can check that out on our CBSSports.com picks page. 


     2. NFL Week 7 picks: Browns improve to 5-2, Chiefs upset SeahawksWelcome to the part of the newsletter where we hand out picks. We have five NFL writers — Pete Prisco, Jordan Dajani, Tyler Sullivan, Jared Dubin and myself — handing out picks each week. I have some big news: For the first time all season, Jared Dubin took home the weekly crown. I don't want to rain on Dubin's parade, but I'm pretty sure the only reason he won is because the rest of us choked the week away. Prisco, Sullivan, and I all finished under .500 for the week while Dajani went 8-6. We basically GAVE Dubin this week's title. I will not be getting Dubin anything for the holidays. That is the only gift he'll be getting from me this year. 
Anyway, if you're new here, here's how things work: I'll give you one Week 7 pick from each writer and then direct you to the rest of their picks for the week. That way, if you like their pick, you can click over and check out all their Week 7 picks; if you hate it, you can ignore the rest and move on with your life.  Pete Prisco — Bengals (+3) 24-23 over Ravens. From Prisco: "The Bengals are coming off a bye, while the Ravens are coming off a loss to the Browns. They could have Lamar Jackson back from an ankle injury here, which certainly changes things. Even if he's back, I think Joe Burrow will have a big day throwing it. The improved Bengals defense will do the rest. Upset." For the rest of Prisco's Week 7 picks, be sure to click here.Tyler Sullivan — Browns (-1.5) 24-17 over Titans. From Sullivan: "The Browns are ... good? They pulled off an upset win over the Lamar Jackson-less Ravens last week and, remarkably, stand in first place in the AFC North heading into Week 7. Deshaun Watson has been clutch this season, as he has four game-winning drives where he's been money. In that window, Watson has completed 75% of his passes (18-of-24), thrown for 179 yards, and has two touchdowns with zero interceptions. To his credit, Cam Ward has also popped in the fourth quarter this season as well, but Tennessee is also tied for the fewest points scored in the NFL over the first three quarters. If that persists, Cleveland has a defense capable of snuffing out any late Ward comeback attempt." For the rest of Sullivan's Week 7 picks, be sure to click here.Jordan Dajani — Steelers 23-20 over Saints (+3.5). From Dajani: "The Steelers are impossible to figure out. From week-to-week — or even half-to-half, as evidenced by last week's overtime victory against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. If you're going to give me the hook at +3.5 in an international game, I'm probably going to take it. The Saints are a perfect 8-0 ATS in their last eight games away from home, and are 3-0 ATS all-time in international games." Dajani's full slate of picks will be released Friday, but you can get a preview here.Jared Dubin — Lions (-3) 34-28 over Packers. From Dubin: "This one has all the makings of a shootout, with two explosive offenses going back and forth. Jared Goff and Co. are coming off the bye, and they have scored 31 or more points in four of their five games to date — and they scored 26 while piling up 452 yards in the other one. Nobody except maybe Kenneth Walker III is doing it at a higher level than Jahmyr Gibbs right now, either. Meanwhile, Green Bay can throw the ball all over the yard, and everyone throws it on the Lions. Maybe Green Bay can actually run with some efficiency in Josh Jacobs' potential return, but it's not like he was all that efficient last season, either. I lean toward the Lions because they can beat you both ways." For the rest of Dubin's Week 7 picks, be sure to click here. John Breech — Chiefs (+2.5) 27-20 over Seahawks. From me: "This is the Kenneth Walker revenge game. Walker is on a personal 15-game winning streak that dates back to last year: He won his final 10 games with the Seahawks, and he's won his first five with Kansas City. All the man does is win, so I certainly will not be picking against him in this spot." For the rest of my Week 7 picks, be sure to click here. For more Week 7 NFL picks, you can check out our CBSSports.com picks page here.   3. NFL Week 7 upset alert: Three favorites who could go down
                                                                    Al Bello/Getty Images
                                                            We saw several big upsets in Week 6, including Arizona's shocking win over the Rams and the Browns' win over the Ravens. There's nothing I love more than a big upset, so I'm hoping those shocking finishes carry over into Week 7. 
So, who should be on upset alert this week? Tyler Sullivan is here to tell us. Giants (+10.5) over Texans. Welcome to the J.J. McCarthy era in New York. I'm genuinely curious to see how this goes for the former Vikings first-round pick, who made his debut last week in the fourth quarter. In that brief showing, McCarthy largely played well, throwing for 243 yards, a touchdown, and an interception. Does this give the Giants a boost? McCarthy will have weapons at his disposal in Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely, and it's possible his rushing ability ignites what has been a lackluster ground attack thus far. Meanwhile,  the Texans will have a slight rest disadvantage here. While they may be home, Houston is fresh off a game in London last Sunday, which could be a factor in this contest. Falcons (+3) over 49ers. At some point, the injuries to San Francisco's wide receiver room have to matter, right? When Mike Evans (Achilles) didn't return for the second half of Monday's matchup against the Commanders, the Niners offense mustered a field goal on the opening possession of the third quarter and then punted three straight times (all three-and-outs) to end the game. With the Week 8 bye right in front of them and San Francisco playing on a short week and on the road, it may behoove them to keep Evans sidelined for this game, with hopes of a two-week break being the remedy for the stretch run. If that turns out to be the case, we got a quick sample of an Evans-less offense for the 49ers, and it wasn't the prettiest. That brings San Francisco down much closer to Atlanta's level and makes them a live home dog. Cardinals (+4.5) over Broncos. It's borderline irresponsible to back the Broncos right now because their offense is totally lost. Bo Nix is averaging just 4.9 air yards per attempt this season, which is the fewest through six games by any player in the last 20 seasons. They won last week despite his performance and the defense taking advantage of some questionable throws by Sam Darnold. Now, they head out on the road to face a Cardinals team that has been pesky this season. Most recently, they held Matthew Stafford and the Rams offense to 16 points in a road win.You can check out Sullivan's full list of possible upsets for Week 7 here. 
    
    

     4. Ranking first-year NFL head coaches: Todd Monken on topIt's been a wild year so far for the NFL's newest head coaches: Five of them are currently in first place or tied for first place, while one of them currently has ZERO wins. There were 10 coaches hired this offseason, and since we're roughly one-third of the way through the season, Garrett Podell has decided it's time to rank how each coach is doing. Here are the top three names in Garrett's ranking: 1. Browns coach Todd Monken. Monken is currently pulling off a miracle: His Browns are in first place in the AFC North in Week 6 or later for the first time since 2014. That's absolutely incredible. There's certainly a smoke-and-mirrors element to it, as the Browns have the worst point differential (-16) among teams with a winning record this season, but wins are wins. 
2. Bills coach Joe Brady. Brady has an unfair advantage among his class of 2026 head-coaching hires because he has been his team's offensive coordinator since 2023. Quarterback Josh Allen leads the NFL in total touchdowns (17), and running back James Cook's 627 yards rushing rank as the third most in the NFL. 3. Ravens coach Jesse Minter. Inheriting two-time NFL MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson is a blessing for new Baltimore head coach Jesse Minter, but he hasn't had him the last two weeks because of an ankle injury. In Week 5, Minter's squad went on the road in primetime and beat the Falcons on "Sunday Night Football" with backup quarterback Tyler Huntley. The Ravens' +24-point differential is the eighth-best in the NFL this season, and they have the same record as the Browns and Steelers atop the AFC North. In news that probably won't surprise you, Dolphins' coach Jeff Hafley, who has ZERO wins so far, is ranked at the bottom of the list. If you want to see where all 10 coaches fall in Garrett's ranking, you'll have to check out his full story here. 
 5. NFL trade deadline: Five players that need a change of scenery
                                                                    Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images
                                                            Don't look now, but the NFL trade deadline (Nov. 10) is just around the corner. We started breaking down some possible trades more than two weeks ago, and we're going to continue that today by taking a look at a few players who could use a change of scenery. Basically, Jordan Dajani came up with a list of five players who probably won't be dealt, but we'd like to see them get moved. 1. Chargers QB Justin Herbert. The Chargers are 0-6, and there's little hope this team can turn it around. Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel is on the hot seat — the same could be said for head coach Jim Harbaugh — and now, injuries are beginning to mount. If quarterback Justin Herbert couldn't figure it out with Ladd McConkey, Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt healthy, what's it going to look like with all of them out/injured? Herbert needs a more comfortable situation — maybe one that includes a Brian Flores defense and Justin Jefferson. 
2. Colts RB Jonathan Taylor. Taylor, on the other hand, has racked up 655 scrimmage yards and seven touchdowns through the first six games of the season. He just became the fastest player to reach 8,000 career rushing yards since Adrian Peterson, and he should be carrying the rock for a team with Super Bowl aspirations. (Note: If you're wondering what teams might be interested in trading for Taylor, we came up with five different trade packages here)3. Raiders EDGE Maxx Crosby. We thought Maxx Crosby got the change of scenery he was after in March, when the Baltimore Ravens agreed to send two first-round picks to the Las Vegas Raiders for their star pass rusher. However, the Ravens backed out of the deal after their doctors allegedly found something worrisome during their in-person physical. I don't know if Crosby still wants out of Vegas. Maybe he viewed the canceled trade as divine intervention signaling he was always meant to don the silver and black. The Raiders are more competitive this year than they have been in quite some time, but I would still like to see Crosby on a winning team. If you want to see Jordan's full list of players who need to be traded, we've got that here. 

    
	

     6. Extra points: NFL punishes three head coaches with near-record finesIt's been a busy few days around the NFL, and since it's nearly impossible to keep track of everything, I put together a quick roundup for you. NFL drops the hammer on three head coaches. Mike Vrabel, Nick Sirianni and Aaron Glenn have all been fined $250,000 by the NFL for their conduct toward game officials. Although they had to pay the fine, all three coaches have been told that they can get their money back if they show good behavior going forward. The NFL is clearly trying to send a message: The fines handed out are the second-largest in league history for any head coach, trailing only the $500,000 fine Bill Belichick received for Spygate. If you want the full story on these near-record fines, we've got all the details here, along with some video of each coach yelling at an official. Giants rolling with J.J. McCarthy at QB this week.  After watching McCarthy throw for 243 yards in the FOURTH QUARTER against the Saints on Sunday, John Harbaugh has seen enough. The Giants coach has announced that McCarthy will not only start this week against the Texans, but he'll likely be the starter after that. "I would never say that anything is permanent in football or life. That's the plan going forward," Harbaugh said. The Giants traded for McCarthy back on Sept. 28, and now, less than a month later, he'll be getting his first start with the team. Vice president attends Bengals practice. JD Vance decided to stop by Bengals' practice on Wednesday after taking part in a campaign rally just north of Cincinnati. You can see some of the footage from his visit here. Vance is a long-time Bengals fan, and when he's not in Washington, D.C., he makes his home in Cincinnati.

body:
Week 7 presents another round of difficult decisions for Fantasy managers, with four teams on bye, injuries reshaping depth charts and several big-name players facing matchups that could limit their production. As we approach the halfway point of the Fantasy regular season, every lineup decision becomes increasingly important.Braelon Allen is among the players worth trusting this week, with Breece Hall's injury opening the door for another strong performance against a vulnerable Dolphins run defense. Meanwhile, Woody Marks could benefit from an expanded workload in Houston, and Bryce Young continues to make a compelling case as a reliable Fantasy starter.On the other side, Patrick Mahomes faces a difficult matchup against Seattle, while Michael Wilson and Jameson Williams carry concerns despite their opportunities in their respective offenses. Even familiar names aren't automatic starts when defensive schemes, playing time and offensive tendencies work against them.That's where Dave Richard's Week 7 matchup breakdown comes in. From defensive coverages and pass-rush pressure to backfield workloads and target distribution, we'll examine the factors that matter most to help you identify trustworthy starters, avoid potential disappointments and make the best possible lineup decisions.

Caleb Williams had two 2-yard runs, had a season low 3.23-second time to throw rate and a season low with Ben Johnson, 3.9-yard average depth of throw against the Falcons last week. That tells me he's still not 100% recovered from his hamstring injury, but it didn't quite turn him into a game manager. Five of his six biggest gains involved him holding the ball for at least three seconds, be it because he moved out of the pocket or not, and that doesn't include his 14-yard touchdown to Colston Loveland, where he escaped pressure and did the whole hold-and-throw-cross-body thing that he seems to live and die by. Williams is dangerous if he's mobile, but his Fantasy upside is lowered if he won't run downfield. The Patriots pass rush has been inconsistent all year but they tend to rack up sacks against statue QBs. Even with a couple of question marks along his O-line, Williams should be able to overcome their pressure and hit targets downfield. Last week, he completed all 26 of his throws for 255 yards when he wasn't pressured. That's bad news for the Patriots and good news for Williams. Luther Burden III had a great stat line last week -- 8-95-0 on eight targets -- but he didn't start, and he played just 39% of the snaps and ran a route on just 44% of Williams' dropbacks, both season lows. This happened because the Bears played with two or more tight ends on 67% of their plays, their second-highest mark of the season. Burden played just five snaps with Colston Loveland and Cole Kmet -- and had his biggest play of the day on one of them! Chicago has leaned into multiple tight end sets in three of their past five games, be it because of weather (Week 2), game script (Week 4), or to give its QB added pass protection (last week). Only the Raiders have felt the need to use a lot of multiple-tight-end formations against the Patriots this season. Because New England ranks 13th in pass-rush pressure rate and 16th in sack rate, the Bears may be more willing to attack downfield with receivers than stack big bodies. That's good news for Burden to keep his target volume flowing, especially since outside receiver Rome Odunze could have his hands full with Pats shutdown cornerback Christian Gonzalez. Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor claimed this week that the Bears "weren't forcing it to (Colston Loveland) or anything like that." Taylor simply said, "The ball found him a couple times," meaning Loveland did what was needed to get open against the Falcons. He also had at least two designed targets, which helps. The Bears have seen man-to-man coverage on just 27 snaps all season, and Williams has yet to even target Loveland in man coverage this year, throwing at him at a 17.5% rate with poor efficiency versus man in 2025. The Patriots have played the second-most man-to-man coverage since Week 2 and third-most on the year, and they especially lean into it on third and short or third and medium downs. The only tight end to get more than 7.5 PPR points against the Pats this year was Brock Bowers. It's a concern when it comes to fully trusting Loveland this week, but you'd have to have some really good alternatives to pull him from lineups.

Aaron Rodgers has leaned into getting the ball out fast and throwing it short over his past two games, resulting in an average depth of target of 4.2 (it was 9.3 through the first four weeks) and a time to throw of 2.46 seconds (it was 2.85 seconds). This was foreseeable last week when he faced the blitz-heavy Bucs, but not in Week 5 against a muted Colts pass rush, nor should it be this way versus New Orleans. That's because the Saints haven't been a blitz-heavy team; they're bottom 10 in blitz pressure rate, bottom five in overall pass rush pressure rate and second-worst in non-blitz pressure rate. If anything, Rodgers should have a little more time to drop back. If he does, DK Metcalf would see the majority of long-distance targets; if/when he doesn't, then Germie Bernard's short-area target parade will continue. It helps Bernard in particular that the Saints play so much zone; he's seen a 24.6% target-per-route-run rate and has a 2.34 yards per route run versus zone since Week 5. I couldn't have been more wrong on Tyler Shough last week, but the Giants defensive gaffes were a big factor. Even though they blitzed like crazy, as expected, the G-Men couldn't tackle or get enough pressure on Shough, and as a result, he found some incredible numbers. The Steelers are a better unit, but not by much. They employ fairly heavy zone coverage each week with a single-high safety lean, but they blitz less than 30% of the time and are bottom-10 in pass rush pressure rate with a modest 7.4% sack rate (boosted by corralling Jalon Daniels five times last week). Those factors might help Shough piece together a solid game, but it'll take an assist from the Steelers missing tackles or drawing penalties for him to post big stats. Shough and the Saints are also expected to be without guard Cesar Ruiz, a great pass blocker. That loss will be felt up front against the Steelers' big boys, and it might mean the Saints ask Juwan Johnson and their other tight ends to chip block a little more. Devaughn Vele has seen a target per route run rate of at least 21% in four of his past five games when facing single-high safety coverage, giving him a chance to bounce back after two stinkers. MUST-START: Chris OlaveSTART: Aaron Rodgers, Jaylen Warren, Germie Bernard & DK Metcalf (low-end No. 2 WRs - Metcalf higher in half and non-PPR), Steelers DST (low-end start)FLEX: Devaughn Vele (PPR flex)SIT: Tyler Shough (high-end No. 2 QB), Juwan Johnson (bye-week TE), Kendre Miller & Alvin Kamara (bye-week RBs), Pat Freiermuth, Bryce Lance, Rico Dowdle, Darnell Washington, Saints DST

Kyle Pitts looks a little more like a tight end and a little less like an explosive athlete these days, but there's plenty of evidence suggesting his role in the Falcons offense is reliable. Since Week 3, his average depth of target has come way down, making him a short-area winner for Michael Penix Jr. In fact, Pitts has had one target longer than 10 air yards in his last three games, so his role is resembling what tight ends in Cleveland did under Kevin Stefanski. That's OK as long as Pitts keeps getting targets -- he's had at least six in each of his past two, including five in the red zone. Only two tight ends this season have seen at least six targets against the 49ers, and both had at least 13.9 PPR points -- both without scoring -- a duo that includes Chig Okonkwo on Monday. I'd be encouraged to try Pitts as a back-end No. 1 TE.

Offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher told the media that the Bengals will scheme up their run game based on what they think will work best against their upcoming opponent. Usually, that's how backfields without a one-star rusher operate, which suggests the Bengals are open to using more Samaje Perine, as they did on shotgun runs at Miami in Week 5. He's not as explosive as Chase Brown, but he is more powerful and could be the back the Bengals lean on to beat up light boxes and/or close out games. Brown remains the better option in the passing game, so it's not like his snaps are going to dry up, but I'd be at least a little nervous about their carries being close to equal when they're not chasing points. The Ravens run defense has been awesome in their past four games against gap-scheme runs (2.5 yards per rush, zero runs of 10-plus yards allowed), and they've also crushed against shotgun runs. If the Bengals take notice, then it means they'll try more zone-scheme stuff and maybe gravitate back toward some under-center carries, two aspects that favor Brown's explosiveness. I would cautiously start Brown as a No. 2 running back, but any runner with the expectation of, say, 18-plus touches and goal-line work should start ahead of him, including Braelon Allen for this week. Sounds like a decent amount of people are still on the fence on Bryce Young. All he's done this season is score at least 23.8 Fantasy points (six-point pass TDs) in all but one game. Touchdowns have boosted him (11 passing in five games), but he's still well in the top half of the league in EPA per dropback, yards per attempt and notably, fourth in pass attempts per game at 40.2. title: Which college football coach will be fired next? The Power Four's hottest seats by tier - CBS Sports

body:
Massive buyouts and soaring roster payrolls have slowed the coaching carousel, but Dave Aranda and Mike Norvell headline a complicated list of names on the hot seat
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    12:01 pm ET

            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Mike Locksley became the first coach fired this season as Maryland made the call to move on Wednesday. But while October is still early to fire a coach, it actually bucks the recent trend. This time last year, there had already been seven FBS coaches fired. Five Power Four coaches were gone by the end of September, with heavy hitters like Penn State's James Franklin, LSU's Brian Kelly and Oklahoma State's Mike Gundy out by October. In all, 30 jobs changed hands in 2025. In many ways, the barrage of firings was the dying embers of an old era. For one, there weren't enough high-level candidates to fill the spots. Michigan hired a stopgap in Kyle Whittingham, and he's floundered. Arkansas whiffed on several choices, and settled for Ryan Silverfield. Penn State missed out on Kalani Sitake and finally had to convince Matt Campbell to leave. Furthermore, college football has changed. While a new coach can help take a program to new heights, pure resource deployment is suddenly the most important factor in the sport. With rosters clearing $30 million regularly, burning a $20 million buyout and having to hire a whole new staff and roster are becoming prohibitive costs. 
In response, we've seen multiple programs try to change their administrative structure to adjust to the new era. Oklahoma and USC rank among programs that hired independent general managers who could realistically last through multiple coaches. It makes for a more NFL-style roster-building approach, where a coach is just one piece of the equation. Last year, we also saw multiple programs try to invest more heavily in coaches to make it work: Wisconsin's Luke Fickell, Florida State's Mike Norvell and Baylor's Dave Aranda, chief among them. Fickell has likely saved his job with the performance, while Aranda and Norvell stay in varying levels of limbo. But still, a $10 million infusion into the roster could prove much more valuable long term than buying out and starting over. Eventually, the market will reset, and we'll see more movement among coaches. It could even happen later this season. But with so much money invested in rosters, college football programs simply cannot afford to spend millions of dead money just to emotionally move off a coach. 
With that in mind, who actually will be the next coach fired in college football? It's a complicated question. The financially prohibitiveCandidates: Mike Norvell, Shane Beamer, Greg SchianoWhen Shane Beamer's Gamecocks lost to No. 24 Kentucky on Oct. 3, it felt like the end. Beamer stood on the sidelines taking in every moment after the overtime loss, and looked defeated in the press conference. Historically, that would be the final moment of an SEC coaching tenure. Instead, reports quickly came out that South Carolina wasn't likely to make a move and that finances were the primary driver. Beamer would be owed more than $22 million if fired after the season, a massive sum as South Carolina tries to fund a major college football roster. 
The situation is even worse at Florida State, where Mike Norvell would be due nearly $50 million. Even for one of the most successful programs of the 21st Century, writing a check like that isn't realistic. Maybe a donor comes forward to underwrite one of these buyouts, but it's hard to see that happening, especially midseason. The complicated endgameCandidates: Dabo Swinney, Deion Sanders, Lincoln RileyAll three of these guys are prohibitively expensive to fire, but separation could prove even more complicated than a simple separation agreement too. 
Swinney is synonymous with Clemson, and the chances of finding a better coach are slim. Sanders has a brand of his own that's bigger than Colorado football, and an acrimonious divorce could cause fissures that last years to come. Riley has the most absurd contract of the bunch, but also has quietly investigated leaving most. It's possible that any of these three figures will leave on their own or reach a mutual understanding, but it will be out of the athletic director's hands. Will they pull the trigger?Candidates: Dave Aranda, Dave Doeren, Bill O'BrienAll three of these coaches are clearly in the hot seat and could easily find themselves on the wrong side depending on how they close out the year. 
Aranda's Bears are sitting at 4-2, but recorded an embarrassing 17-6 loss to rival TCU at home and close the year with BYU, Texas Tech and Houston. With the promise of this roster, and a manageable buyout, 7-5 won't cut it. Doeren is 3-3, with a loss to Vanderbilt that continues to look worse, but the Wolfpack also upset Louisville. If he can get back to bowl eligibility, that might be enough, but donors could also be ready to move on. Will they invest enough to attract a better candidate? The same is true of O'Brien, who has settled down after upsetting Pittsburgh a week ago. Find two more wins on a fairly manageable schedule, and he should be fine. 
Played themselves offCandidates: Bill Belichick, Jeff Lebby, Luke FickellNorth Carolina, Mississippi State and Wisconsin all decided to invest far more money into the programs during this cycle, and it paid off in a big way. The Tar Heels are 4-2 and gave both Clemson and Notre Dame tough games. There should be at least three more wins on the schedule. Kamario Taylor completely changed the trajectory of Lebby's tenure at Mississippi State. The Bulldogs could push for eight wins with their schedule. Since the second half against Notre Dame, Wisconsin has looked the part during a 4-2 start. A loss to UCLA will stick in their craw, but there are at least four wins remaining too. All three of these cases provide credence to the idea that changing the context around a coach can quickly turn fortunes.

title: Clippers coach Ty Lue dedicates opening night win to suspended Steve Ballmer - CBS Sports
description: Lue made sure to shoutout the Clippers' suspended owner after beating the Kings
body:
Lue made sure to shoutout the Clippers' suspended owner after beating the Kings
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:06 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Clippers began the 2026-27 season on Wednesday with a 121-96 blowout win over the Kings in a battle of teams projected to finish at the bottom of the Western Conference this season. The Clippers, following a tumultuous offseason, hope to surprise in the West and contend for a play-in spot. And after beating the Kings, coach Tyronn Lue dedicated the win to Steve Ballmer, the Clippers owner who is suspended for the year after the NBA found the team guilty of violating salary cap circumvention rules involving Kawhi Leonard. "That win was for Mr. Ballmer," Lue said with a smile. "Just want to say thank you for everything. We're still fighting for him."
The NBA's investigation found "a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations" by the Clippers, who were deemed to have "affirmatively initiated off-court income opportunities" and facilitated "endorsement agreements" between Leonard and four companies. As a result, the Clippers forfeited five first-round picks and were fined $30 million while Ballmer and two other team executives were suspended. Leonard has since been traded to the Raptors.
During the suspension, which was handed down in September, Ballmer, known for his boisterous presence courtside at Clippers home games, is banned from all league and team activities. Lue called Ballmer "one of the best men I know," while Clippers guard Darius Garland said Ballmer was "here in spirit.""We keep him in our hearts," Lue said. "He provided a great living for everyone in this arena. One of the best men that I know, so we definitely want to dedicate this one to him tonight."The Clippers' upcoming schedule is brutal with the Lakers (twice), Thunder, Timberwolves, Warriors and Raptors coming up, so Lue was able to take advantage of the moment for this shoutout after beating the Kings. 
The Clippers face a long road back to contention after losing five future first-round picks as part of the punishment, but Lue seems locked in for the long haul in L.A. and made sure to show some love to the Clippers big boss after the win.

title: Bruno Fernandes' rebellion in Como underlines Man United's never-ending problem - CBS Sports
description: Eight managers since Sir Alex Ferguson have lost the players, and until there are significant changes, the ninth
body:
Eight managers since Sir Alex Ferguson have lost the players, and until there are significant changes, the ninth will too
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    11:13 am ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        "Sire, it is said that the Manchester United players are revolting." "You said it, they stink on ice." And they're not much better on turf either.The rabble inside the Old Trafford dressing room has been roused. Their rebellion will rage on until it ends the same way every other one does. The great ruler will dismiss himself of some unwise counsellor or another. Though it has been suggested he is safe for the time being, it is hard to see a future that does not end with sheriff Michael Carrick being run out of town. Chancellor Jason Wilcox will find himself in a hairy situation. The banishments will come with promises that the realm's most loyal subjects will never be so mistreated again. Their cries have been heard.And then the cycle will begin again.After all, the only shared trait of the eight men to have taken on a meaningful run of Manchester United games since Sir Alex Ferguson's retirement is that the players have turned on them. Bruno Fernandes' open disgruntlement of Michael Carrick is not even that unique, bringing to mind Cristiano Ronaldo's withering, petulant dismissal of Erik ten Hag two years ago.The club that employed football management's last great authoritarian have spent more than a decade dripping the same message to the first team. The guy who picks the team, he is accountable to you. You will outlast him. He will bear the consequences of your actions. That is not to argue that Michael Carrick is remotely blameless for United's faltering start to the season, let alone the game plan at Como.Fernandes was not wrong in his assessment that allowing Nico Paz, Martin Baturina and Jacobo Ramon the space and time to pick a pass was probably going to imbue a very capable opponent with confidence. He was of course wrong to air those concerns in front of television cameras. Far further beyond the pale, however, was what appeared to be Fernandes' refusal to play along to the plan that Carrick had assigned to his side.

                                                                    UEFA
                                                            With less than 26 minutes played, Fernandes failed to control a pass from Mason Mount as Ramon closed in, the sort of error that was at least partially on the receiver. Como now had possession on the edge of the attacking third. In response, the United captain threw his hands up in frustration. The camera drifted away from him for a moment, following the ball in a way that Fernandes wasn't.When he returned to the shot, with Mount tangling with Baturina as he and Paz attempted to break into the area, Fernandes was still walking. Como's possession went backwards and yet United's most advanced player was looking the other way. Maximo Perrone is scanning the pitch as he receives possession, a little check over the shoulder presumably showing to the Argentine that the No. 8 in white was no threat. A second later, Fernandes is picking at his boots. 
                                                                    UEFA
                                                            A third of the game was gone, and yes, United probably were playing to the wrong game plan. Then again, teams set themselves up in the wrong way all across the world every week and find a way to win football matches. Most of those do not have players of the quality of Fernandes, Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha. The collective tends to trump the individual in this sport but Fernandes is one of the best individuals. If he sets his mind to it, he can at least give his opponents an almighty challenge no matter if the circumstances are aligned against him.
"Whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run and you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren't going to win," said Carrick afterwards, in what in that moment seemed to be his final press conference. For the time being, he remains, due to face the media again ahead of Sunday's visit of Bournemouth to Old Trafford. Should United choose to make a managerial change, CBS Sports sources indicate that Antonio Conte would be open to talks over the vacancy.Would anything really change with a new man in the dugout? Perhaps in the short term. There are quick tactical fixes that a Carrick successor could make, among them sorting out a shot diet that indulges the likes of Fernandes swinging from bad positions outside the penalty area.
Really though, bigger change is required than that which can be engendered by any head coach. If a leader as mild-mannered and measured as Carrick is unable to keep his players from venting their spleen on a weekly basis, then the dressing room is unsalvageable. That Fernandes had a point last week does not really matter. Nor does it that there was barely a word misspoken by Lisandro Martinez last week when he called out director of football Jason Wilcox and those who employ him. Far be it for this column to argue against players speaking their mind to the media but a confident organisation should feel able to hold its employees to account. It has been suggested that United will activate the option in Martinez's contract to preserve his value. What message does that send to the next player who might have something to say about Carrick, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the Old Trafford support or whatever else they take issue with? Publicly airing your issues with your employers comes with no financial consequences. In fact, in Martinez's case, you're straight back in the XI on the weekend.This is Augean stables stuff. A cleansing is required. But of course the problem in Elis was never the cattle, per se. It was the ruler who had gone 30 years without getting the cleaners in. So long as the Glazers and Ratcliffe continue in their current fashion, there will be Fernandeses, Martinezes and Ronaldos trying and failing to clean house.

title: These 7 stretch run storylines will define the second half of the 2026 season - CBS Sports
description: This week, CBS Sports has been celebrating the midpoint of the 2026 college football season. We have honored the best and brightest with
body:
This week, CBS Sports has been celebrating the midpoint of the 2026 college football season. We have honored the best and brightest with a Midseason All-America Team, given the experts a chance to redo their predictions for how the season will end in the College Football Playoff, and taken the time to offer a midseason report card for every power conference team.The key word here is celebrate, because while it's easy to get caught up in complaining about a coach, quarterback or playoff format, college football still overwhelms us with names, games and storylines worth debating and celebrating every week. When there's a chaotic Saturday like in Week 7 with five of the top seven teams going down in a 12-hour span, we celebrate it. It hasn't mattered whether we had poll champions, BCS champions or any number of playoff formats; those stories have been a driving reason behind college football's popularity.But to be fair to complaining as an institution, complaining is nothing new in college football.We complain about the quarterback who can't convert on deep passes, the offensive coordinator who isn't calling the right plays and the defense that just can't get off the field on third down. We complain about officials (a lot) and lightning delays (seemingly a lot more than we used to).
Complaining has also driven a lot of the changes in college football. It both brought about the BCS after years of split champions and then tore it down, leading to the four-team CFP that was soon expanded again after complaints about access. The cries for "more" and "now" seem to have us headed for another change, kickstarting a visceral response of complaints about the impact of expansion.I know college football needs debates, hypotheticals and yes, even some complaints to fuel the conversation around the sport. But I also know that it's not fair to the players, coaches, staffers and families to overload the conversation with complaining -- especially if it takes away from the celebrating.College football in 2026 has been a blast, and the second half of the season is going to pack even more of a punch. Getting to watch, talk and think about this sport is such a privilege; we'd hate to see anyone waste that privilege on complaining. The sport's suits can figure out playoff formats and roster caps in boardrooms on someone else's dime, because right now we're only focusing on the storylines that will drive the action on the field during the stretch run of the 2026 season. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    How will Ohio State respond to Julian Sayin's injury?Ryan Day's outlook on Julian Sayin's recovery suggests that any projection for the Buckeyes must include the possibility, if not the likelihood, that he won't make it back this season. No one has attempted to set a timetable yet, but if we're trying to make our midseason predictions, you must consider that it's either going to be Luke Fahey or Tavien St. Clair as QB1 in key games down the stretch against USC, Oregon, Northwestern, Nebraska and Michigan. Did you notice that list of five opponents? They're all top-50 teams, and their current combined record is 24-8. Every single one of the remaining games is losable individually for Ohio State, but the Buckeyes' track record suggests the standard is too high to let the entire team fall apart with one injury. This is the program, after all, that was down to its third quarterback when Cardale Jones stepped up to lead a national title run in 2014-15. Something is undeniably lost with Julian Sayin's talent and the experience he's gained from the high-level games of the two seasons, but Ohio State is among the few programs you'd still trust to endure the setback and have a shot at winning it all if it can make the CFP. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    A boiling point in Austin for Steve Sarkisian and Arch ManningIt's always something with Texas. It's the playcalling, the injuries, the turnovers or any number of reasons why the Longhorns have not been meeting their expectations since the start of last season. Texas reached the CFPsemifinals in both the 2023 and 2024 seasons, so the transition to the Arch Manning era was expected to unlock the next step in its bid to win it all. Texas finishing last season in the Cheez-It Bowl with a roster built to win it all was a disappointment, and having two losses through seven weeks suggests 2026 could also be a disappointment. Not all is lost in Austin for Sark and Arch, but the margin for error is razor thin, and the road ahead includes plenty of landmines. Because Arch, Sark and the Longhorns had that incredible comeback win against Ohio State, there is a built-in bonus to how Texas will be viewed as an at-large candidate for the CFP. But with Ole Miss coming to town on Saturday and road trips to Missouri and LSU in November, there are more than a couple of obvious spots where the Longhorns could take another loss. If the offense does not take a significant step forward with the pressure being at its peak, things could get really uncomfortable in Austin.  
Sorting winners and losers from the eventual SEC logjam There are nine teams currently in the AP Top 25 poll from the SEC, and odds suggest that half of them (four or five) will end up making the College Football Playoff. The most enticing and anxiety-riddled storyline for many rabid fan bases is who will win the remaining pivotal matchups that will set this chaotic SEC race in motion. Consider that Kentucky already has a win against LSU but a loss to Alabama, which has losses to Tennessee and Georgia, as well as that win against the Wildcats. The criss-crossing nature of these head-to-head contradictions could fill a conspiracy theory board, but we're going to try and isolate the most important matchups in the SEC and CFP race. Georgia vs. Florida (Oct. 31) Alabama at LSU (Nov. 7) Georgia at Ole Miss (Nov. 7) Kentucky at Tennessee (Nov. 7) Texas vs. Missouri (Nov. 7) Texas at LSU (Nov. 14) Florida at Kentucky (Nov. 14) Missouri at Georgia (Nov. 14) LSU at Tennessee (Nov. 21)   Kentucky at Missouri (Nov. 21) It's simple enough to explain but emotionally exhausting to consider. These 10 games are likely to determine, through both their own head-to-head results and tiebreaker implications, who gets to play in the SEC Championship Game and who makes the CFP. The teams that lose more of these games than they win will be celebrating the traditional bowl system as we know it for at least one more year, while the winners will have advantages as long as they handle business in their remaining games. 
Of course, last week's results and our knowledge of the shrinking talent gap tell us no game is a layup, especially in the SEC. But those 10 games set up now as a good watch list for how the winners will separate themselves in a conference crowded with contenders. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Collision Course, Part 1: Miami and Notre Dame Miami just took over the No. 1 spot in the college football rankings, setting up a couple of weekends where the Hurricanes get to live in the rarefied air of the top spot. It's a position that Miami has not held since 2002, so we really don't have a sense of what "The U" looks like in the modern era, carrying the expectations of being the best team in the country. The Hurricanes will start by testing that status against a Pitt team without its star quarterback, and then on the road against Bill Belichick and North Carolina. But if Miami can navigate through those two foes without a misstep, then it sets up a colossal collision in South Bend against Notre Dame. 
The fact that Miami and Notre Dame are running hot at the same time is a welcome renewal of a rivalry that once defined the national championship conversation. And after last season's Miami-Notre Dame CFP rankings flip-flop, this latest chapter in the rivalry includes drama and revenge.  The fact that Notre Dame has already lost once this season only raises the stakes of that Nov. 7 showdown, which will serve as a "prove-it" moment for the Fighting Irish in the eyes of the Selection Committee. With the Big 12 looking heavy at the top and a pack of SEC teams carrying good non-conference wins, Notre Dame could benefit greatly from having a high-quality win to secure an at-large bid. Collision Course, Part 2: USC at UCLA 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    
                            
    
                                                
                    
    USC and UCLA are both in the top four of the Big Ten standings through four games, each with a fair shot at competing for a Big Ten title and a spot in the CFP. Yet the outlook for both teams, a combined 7-1 in league play, comes with injury concerns and the uncertainty of a tougher stretch ahead in the second half of the schedule. 
USC still has to play Ohio State and Indiana while UCLA has a more manageable path, but the Bruins (like Ohio State) are keeping their CFP hopes alive with a backup quarterback. Ty Diefenbach stepped in for Nico Iamaleava effectively in the win over Oregon and led the team to a victory over Wisconsin. But UCLA's playoff hopes will ride on its run game and defense, which together set a high floor for what the Bruins can accomplish without Nico. USC's injury issues have hit most positions other than quarterback, with offensive linemen going down early and pass catchers swapping in and out throughout the first weeks of the season. The off week should provide some help on that front, but we await to see just how healthy the team is when USC returns to action in Week 8. Gary Patterson is going to need his defense, which has had a good October against a pair of struggling offenses, to create the same game-changing plays against much tougher competition in the weeks ahead. 
For UCLA, you have Year 1 Bob Chensey putting together a Coach of the Year argument, while on the other side of town Lincoln Riley is in Year 5 and still looking for his first CFP appearance with the Trojans. UCLA is 6-0 overall and 4-0 in Big Ten play while USC is 5-1 overall and 3-1 in Big Ten play, but any hopeful postseason path for both likely needs a win against the other. That breathes new life into this crosstown rivalry, and ramps up the pressure on one of these coaches to make a statement when they meet on the field on Nov. 28.     A Royal Rumble in the Big 12 Big 12 commissioner Brett Yormark has said his conference is "in the events business" and even struck a deal with WWE to award a wrestling-style title belt to the winner of the Big 12 title game. Well, Commissioner Yormark, may I suggest a Royal Rumble? Maybe a four-way ladder match to determine who will emerge as the conference champion? Because right now we have four stellar Big 12 teams, all sitting inside the top 15 of the AP Top 25 poll, and not a ton of cross-over on the schedule to give us head-to-head results. No. 8 Texas Tech already has a great win against No. 14 Houston, but will not face BYU or Utah in the regular season. From that perspective, the Red Raiders have pulled their weight and now just need to handle business the rest of the way. 
No. 10 Utah has yet to play a top-50 team, but the Utes will have their time with a visit from Houston this weekend and then the Holy War rivalry against BYU on Nov. 7. And No. 2 BYU, which very clearly has one of the best wins in the country after beating Notre Dame, similarly does not play Houston or Texas Tech but will clash with rival Utah early next month. That absence of crossover results will create a real headache in figuring out both who will make the Big 12 title game and which teams deserve the best spots in the CFP. The bad news for the SEC, Big Ten and ACC is that a lot of preseason projections saw the Big 12 as a one-bid league, but with four teams in the top 15 and three in the top 10 at the midseason point, we've got a decent chance the conference finds itself with as many as three teams in the final bracket. Who joins Maryland on the Coaching Carousel? Maryland officially ended the Mike Locksley era this week, parting ways with the coach who had been leading the Terps since the 2019 season. It's the first power conference job to open in the 2026-27 cycle, and has prompted some larger conversations about what kind of spinning we should expect from the coaching carousel. Last season, we had UCLA, Virginia Tech, Arkansas and Penn State all open at this point in the calendar, and LSU would soon follow suit before the end of October. Auburn opened in early November, followed by Florida and eventually Kentucky and Michigan State as well. With so many power conference jobs changing hands last year, the thought (at least through a quiet September on the coaching carousel) was that we would see less coaching carnage this go around. All eyes are on Mike Norvell at Florida State, as the Seminoles' effort and performances seem to be a week-to-week indicator of his hot-seat status, but both in Tallahassee and in several spots around the country, the appetite to make a change is being questioned. If Shane Beamer, Luke Fickell and Dave Doeren are able to throw a few more signature wins on the card, we could see a lot of those names from the hot seat outlook back for 2027. There is, however, a path for this coaching carousel to get very silly, but it will need a few more disappointing results and boatloads of money. There are larger, existential questions at blue blood programs like USC and Texas, which, as we discussed above, are under immense pressure to contend for championships with high-dollar rosters and high-dollar coaches. Those coaches would demand equally expensive buyouts, so it would take some serious disappointment to motivate the financial commitment to a change. But if you want to know how a quiet coaching carousel turns into a frenzy, it would start with one of those schools deciding to join Maryland on the ride.

title: Big 12 midseason grades: BYU earns 'A++,' Deion Sanders and Colorado get 'D' - CBS Sports
description: The Big 12 has produced countless chaotic seasons over the years, but this group could be one of the craziest yet. Heading into the year
body:
The Big 12 has produced countless chaotic seasons over the years, but this group could be one of the craziest yet. Heading into the year, zero conference teams ranked in the AP Top 10. Now, three teams are there, with Houston close behind. The league's strength at the top has been a major storyline after BYU stunned Notre Dame to move to No. 2. No. 8 Texas Tech and No. 10 Utah also stand poised to compete for the postseason. Down the list, though, there's been some real spiciness. Oklahoma State overcame an early loss to Tulsa to stun Oregon and enter the conference title race. Baylor shook off a 5-7 campaign to start 4-2. Arizona continues to take steps forward under third-year coach Brent Brennan. With that in mind, here's how we grade every Big 12 team at the midway point. There were only four As given out, but plenty of encouraging signs. 

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 25 ArizonaRecord: 5-1, 2-1 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Wildcats lost an early matchup on the road against BYU. After their win over Notre Dame, that's perfectly defensible. Other than that game, the Wildcats have been fantastic, winning every game by double digits and remaining in the Big 12 title race. Quarterback Noah Fifita is putting together his best-ever effort, and the Wildcats have a shot to shock the conference in two weeks when they travel to Lubbock. Grade: A-
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Arizona StateRecord: 3-3, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Sun Devils knew there would be some work to do after replacing several key playmakers, but the collapse has been far worse than expected. Arizona State allowed 108 points over its last two Big 12 games and will now make a quarterback change, going from Cutter Boley to veteran Mikey Keene. A win over Kansas will keep the Sun Devils out of the Big 12's cellar, but a bowl game isn't likely. Grade: D
                            
    
                                                
                    
    BaylorRecord: 4-2, 2-1 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Bears are hard to grade after the first several weeks. The roster is clearly better, especially on defense, holding every opponent this season to 20 or fewer points. But after an embarrassing 17-6 loss to TCU, the possibility of moving out of the middle class seems unlikely. Is that enough to save Dave Aranda's job? Grade: C+

                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 2 BYURecord: 6-0, 3-0 | Preseason AP ranking: 14What more can you say? BYU is No. 2 in the country for the first time since 1984 and just stunned Notre Dame on their home field. Quarterback Bear Bachmeier is a Heisman contender. Kalani Sitake is the envy of college football. There's no grading scale on earth that could possibly capture what this season has been for BYU. Grade: A++
                            
    
                                                
                    
    UCFRecord: 3-3, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Knights have put together a strong defensive effort, but for the second year in a row, the offense is struggling through injuries. It's a testament to the roster that UCF has managed to stay competitive against some of the best teams in the Big 12. Can they get back on track when they return quarterback Alonza Barnett? Grade: C
                            
    
                                                
                    
    CincinnatiRecord: 4-2, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Bearcats started 4-0 with a win over Kansas State, but losses by 27 points to Arizona and in a barn burner to West Virginia put a damper on it. Over the next three weeks, Cincinnati plays No. 8 Texas Tech, No. 10 Utah and No. 14 Houston, and then closes with No. 2 BYU. Is a bowl game guaranteed? Grade: C+

                            
    
                                                
                    
    ColoradoRecord: 2-4, 0-3 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Buffaloes had another messy roster, and the results have followed. A 27-24 loss against No. 11 Utah was perhaps the best result of the season because blowouts against Texas Tech and Northwestern didn't help. Colorado is likely heading for the bottom of the Big 12 again. Grade: D
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 14 HoustonRecord: 6-1, 3-1 | Preseason AP ranking: 23Willie Fritz is a turnaround artist, and the Cougars are officially turned around. Houston broke into the AP Top 15, and their only loss was a tough road trip against Texas Tech in Week 3. Quarterback Conner Weigman took a massive step forward, and the defense continues to play well. Everything is coming up Coogs. Grade: A
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Iowa StateRecord: 3-3, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe record may not show it, but Iowa State has been a nice surprise in the Big 12. The Cyclones lost every starter from last year's team to graduation or transfer, but Jimmy Rogers did a sensational job restocking through the transfer portal. 
Iowa State is 3-3, but all three losses came against ranked opponents, and each was at least mildly competitive. It doesn't get much easier with No. 25 Arizona and Oklahoma State in the next two weeks, but don't be surprised if the Cyclones fly high in November. Grade: B
                            
    
                                                
                    
    KansasRecord: 2-4, 0-3 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThere's just not much to write home about during a transitional season for the Jayhawks. Quarterback Isaiah Marshall is explosive, but not consistent. The defense has shown moments, but not enough. Kansas is 0-4 against Power Four opponents, but has competed in every game. Grade: D+

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Kansas StateRecord: 4-2, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AThe Wildcats showed signs of life in nonconference play, but everything has crashed back to earth in Big 12 play. A road loss to Cincinnati was an early warning sign and Houston flattened the Wildcats. Kansas State was at least able to pull off a comeback to beat rival Kansas by 11 points, but this team is far from contention. Grade: C-
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Oklahoma StateRecord: 4-2, 2-1 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AComing off 1-11 in Mike Gundy's final season, Oklahoma State is right back on track under first-year coach Eric Morris. The Cowboys have the best offense in the Big 12 behind superstar quarterback Drew Mestemaker and have one of the most impressive wins in the conference against Oregon. Tough losses to Tulsa and Houston prevent an A, but the Cowboys are in great shape. Grade: B+

                            
    
                                                
                    
    TCURecord: 3-3, 1-2 | Preseason AP ranking: N/AIt's been a strange season for TCU, which came into the season with expectations of contending. The Horned Frogs lost their first three Power Four games, but all were by one score. Beating rival Baylor helps bring some good vibes to a program that's been legitimately impressive on defense, but handling business and getting back to a bowl game will help quiet the waters. Grade: D+
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 8 Texas TechRecord: 6-0, 3-0 | Preseason AP ranking: 12It's a testament to the new standard in Lubbock that a second straight 6-0 start for the first time in program history is a little disappointing. 
The Red Raiders are in the bottom half of the conference in both total offense and defense and have struggled to produce consistent play. They also have an impressive win over Houston. If they can handle Cincinnati and Arizona in the next two weeks, the Red Raiders are a firm A. Grade: B+
                            
    
                                                
                    
    No. 10 UtahRecord: 6-0, 3-0 | Preseason AP ranking: 21The Utes haven't played anyone yet, but they've been one of the most dominant teams in the Big 12 when they've taken the field. Utah beat five of its six opponents by at least two touchdowns as the Morgan Scalley era gets off to an impeccable start. Utah can bump their grade to a full A with a win over Houston this week. Grade: A-

                            
    
                                                
                    
    West VirginiaRecord: 4-3, 1-3 | Preseason AP ranking: N/ARich Rodriguez played roster roulette for the second straight year, and found some real hits. Quarterback Michael Hawkins Jr. and running back Cam Cook have turned into a new-age Pat White and Steve Slaton, jumping up to No. 2 in the Big 12 in total offense. The defense however… not great. But still, getting back to a winning record and real competitiveness would be a great Year 2. Grade: B

title: Miami president discusses moving to SEC, Big Ten or going independent - CBS Sports
description: Miami president Joe Echevarria says his school is a 'proud member of the ACC' but is open to conference realignme
body:
Miami president Joe Echevarria says his school is a 'proud member of the ACC' but is open to conference realignment talks
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 22, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:19 am ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        As the Protect College Sports Act awaits its fate in the House of Representatives, the top programs in the ACC are fighting for changes that would stop another round of conference expansion and make it harder for member teams to leave for the Big Ten or the SEC. Among the schools leading the charge to change the expansion cap provision in the bill is the University of Miami, where president Joe Echevarria doesn't mince words about the Hurricanes' desire to be part of college football's elite. Echevarria discussed the Hurricanes' future plans in an extremely candid interview with Yahoo Sports. He explained that their desire to join the SEC or Big Ten has nothing to do with displeasure with the ACC, but rather the realities of the current college football landscape -- bluntly saying "we sit in the second tier." "You cannot lock us into a conference," Echevarria says. "The fact is that we won about every game you could win last year and maxed out in revenue in our current [ACC] sharing model. And we made the same amount of money as other institutions [in the Big Ten and SEC] whose football programs operate at different levels of investment and performance."
The financial reality of modern college football is that the gap between the teams in the SEC and Big Ten and those outside -- even in the other two Power Four conferences -- is going to grow. The widening revenue splits between the conferences will only exacerbate the challenge of keeping up spending for those in the ACC and Big 12. For a program like Miami, they simply want to be in a conference where everyone else is as committed to spending as they are.As for where Miami would like to go, Echevarria waded into waters few school officials would on the record and explained why the Big Ten is an ideal fit academically, while the SEC obviously lines up geographically. "As an AAU [Association of American Universities] research institution, we line up with the Big Ten's profile," he says. "We have an exceptionally strong profile that compares favorably with leading research institutions across the country. On the geography idea, we line up better with the SEC."
The geography bit may also not be that big of a hurdle for the Big Ten, given that the conference already stretches coast-to-coast. Adding Miami could be intriguing for a conference that's only really lacking a footprint in the Southeast at this point, while the SEC already has a presence in the state with Florida. As Miami, Florida State, Clemson, North Carolina and others push to raise the conference expansion cap in the bill from 20 teams to 22, paving an easier path for the ACC's best to leave, Echevarria explained the Hurricanes are also considering what Plan B looks like if that next round of conference realignment doesn't happen. "If we have to go independent, I like our chances because we are a national brand," Echevarria says. "I wouldn't like to do that because scheduling [other sports] is really tough. It's great for football but what about track, volleyball and the golf team?"
Conference realignment discussions rarely happen publicly, largely because if they fall apart, you run the risk of upsetting your current conference. However, that Band-Aid has already been ripped off by the top teams in the ACC, who have sued the conference to create a better exit fee structure, and the growing gap in spending between the top and bottom -- in both football and basketball -- makes it clear what programs are and aren't willing to chase that elite status. If there were any question of Miami's desire to get out of the ACC, Echevarria made it clear with his incredibly candid commentary on the situation. Now it's just a matter of waiting and seeing regarding the PCSA and the fallout from it either passing or failing to advance into law.

title: Three reasons why the Rays can finally win their first World Series title - CBS Sports

body:
The Rays, the AL's best team throughout 2026, will try to win their first ring vs. the Brewers in their third WS trip

        The Tampa Bay Rays, even though they won a robust 98 games during the regular season and bested the New York Yankees in the American League East race, are going to be underdogs in the World Series. That's because they're running up against the Milwaukee Brewers, who during the regular season won more games than the Rays and put up a much better run differential, all against a tougher schedule. "Underdog," however, does not mean "fated to lose," especially in a sport like baseball and just as especially when the Rays are such a strong team in their own rights. Any team is capable of beating any other in this sport, and in this instance, a Rays series win would be barely a mild upset. Now, it's hard to say the two teams are perfectly evenly matched, but they're not far from it, really. On that note, let's have a quick look at why the Rays may indeed be poised to win the World Series that lurks before us. 1. They have a potential edge at the front of the rotationDrew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta have been stellar in OctoberYes, the Brewers have the one-two punch of Jacob Misiorowski, the NL Cy Young favorite, and rookie standout Logan Henderson, but the Rays boast Drew Rasmussen and deadline addition (and ALCS MVP) Freddy Peralta, the former Brewer stalwart. On paper, you'd lean Brewers on this front, but consider these rotation fronts have fared in the postseason thus far: PitchersIPERAK/BBMisiorowski and Henderson17 ⅓3.121.89Rasmussen and Peralta37 ⅔1.193.50By no means has the Milwaukee tandem been bad, at least on the run-prevention front, but Rasmussen and Peralta have been much better in these playoffs. Of particular concern is Misiorowski's and Henderson's struggles at the command-and-control level, as measured by K/BB ratio. Yes, this may be the small sample size at work, but it's also possible that the much younger Brewers rotation front is hitting a workload wall. Last season, Misiorowski – minors, majors, and playoffs combined – worked 141 ⅓ innings. In 2026, his regular-season and postseason innings tally is up to 183. That's a big jump, especially for a guy who's thrown, oh, almost 1,200 triple-digit fastballs on the year. He hasn't had a true ace-level start in more than a month. As for Henderson, he's also seen a sizable innings jump – from 103 innings, Triple-A and the majors combined, in 2025 to 131 ⅓ this season, Triple-A, majors, and postseason combined. None of these are irresponsible leaps forward or anything like that, but turning a six-month season into a seven-month season can be a challenge for any pitcher, especially a young one. On the other side, Rasmussen and Peralta are older and, especially in Peralta's case, familiar with high workloads and the stamina and durability those workloads require. If the series goes long enough, each of these one-two punches will make a total of four starts. As such, this potential edge for Tampa Bay could be a real difference-maker. On another level, the presence of Nick Martinez in the Rays rotation could be another possible edge once Game 3 rolls around. 2. They're a different team since the trade deadlineThe Rays have gone 40-20 (and 7-2 in the playoffs) since the trade deadlineThe Rays made some key additions leading up to this year's trade deadline, and those additions raised the ceiling for this team. Peralta's recent merits are noted above, and after being acquired from the Mets, he made some adjustments and registered a 131 ERA+ in 10 stretch-drive starts. He's been even better than that lately. Acquiring Liam Hicks from the Marlins – a fairly bold maneuver, since contenders typically don't like to switch primary catchers in the middle of the season – also paid off. The underrated Hicks batted .288/.379/.440 for Tampa Bay after the trade and thus drastically upgraded the position. He was Kevin Cash's No. 3 hitter in the clincher over Cleveland. Elsewhere, right-handed reliever Tyler Wells has improved the Rays' setup depth – a pronounced need leading up to the deadline. In at least somewhat related matters, the Rays since the deadline are 40-20, counting the postseason to date. 3. They have the best hitter in the seriesJunior Caminero owns a series-altering bat
Sometimes in a postseason series, one player is capable of taking over, and Rays third baseman Junior Caminero is the leading threat to do just that. During the regular season, Caminero – in his age-22 campaign – played in every game, put up an OPS+ of 144, and smacked 42 homers. In 2025, he hit 45 homers. Backing it up is some of the best quality-of-contact indicators in all of baseball. He's an elite hitter, and no one in this series is more likely than he is to take over a game, and perhaps a series, with his bat-work.
